title: What is Apache Spark?
dek: Start with the problem Spark solves, before the API you write.
idea: Spark is a distributed compute engine. Your data is divided into partitions, and work on those partitions can run in parallel.

sections.title: Why distributed processing?
sections.body:
Imagine computing daily revenue from a year of transaction events. On a laptop, the data may exceed available memory or take longer than your processing window. A distributed engine coordinates work across machines. That coordination has a cost: a small CSV may be simpler and faster to process with pandas or a database.

The useful interview question is: what limits this workload—data size, CPU, I/O, or latency? “Big data” alone is not a sizing decision.

sections.title: Compute is different from storage
sections.body: Spark reads data, computes results, and writes them to a destination. Your source might be object storage or a database; Spark itself is not your permanent database. Storage, table formats, and compute are separate choices.

sections.title: A small example, a useful habit
sections.body: Start with a tiny dataset whose result you can calculate yourself. Here, two successful payments total ₹1,200. The same expression can later operate over partitioned production data. This example assumes a spark session; the next lesson explains its architecture.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
payments = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("success", 500), ("failed", 200), ("success", 700)],
    "status string, amount long"
)
revenue = (payments.filter(F.col("status") == "success")
           .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))
revenue.show()
pitfall: Spark does not require every dataset to fit in RAM. Distributed processing is also not automatically faster for small workloads.
question: Would you use Spark to process a 20 MB CSV every morning?
answer: First check existing infrastructure, transformations, and latency requirements. A local script or SQL engine may be enough. Spark can still make sense if the pipeline already runs there, but distributed overhead needs a reason.

title: Driver, executors & the cluster
dek: Know who plans the work and who actually runs it.
idea: The driver coordinates your application. Executors run tasks and hold application data. The cluster manager allocates resources.

sections.title: Three roles to keep separate
sections.body: The driver plans and schedules work. The executors are application processes that run tasks. A cluster manager, such as YARN, Kubernetes, or Spark standalone, provides resources. A worker machine is not the same thing as an executor process.

sections.title: Where does your Python run?
sections.body: In classic PySpark, your Python program communicates with Spark’s JVM machinery. Python UDFs can involve Python worker processes on executors. Built-in DataFrame expressions generally execute through Spark’s engine; writing Python syntax does not mean every row runs through Python.

sections.title: Think about the destination
sections.body: A distributed operation can finish successfully and still overwhelm the driver if you bring back too much data. When debugging, inspect a bounded sample and the Spark UI. Ask which process ran out of memory before suggesting more executor memory.

code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("local[2]")  # two local task threads, not two executors
         .appName("spark-fieldnotes")
         .getOrCreate())
spark.range(10).show(5)
output: Shows IDs 0–4, followed by a notice that only five rows are shown.
pitfall: local[2] is a local learning setup, not a two-machine cluster. In production, deployment configuration determines where the driver runs.
question: The driver crashes after collect(), but executors have free memory. Why?
answer: collect() returns all rows to the driver. Diagnose the driver result size and heap rather than only executor capacity. Keep processing distributed, write results to storage, or inspect a bounded sample.

title: RDDs, DataFrames & Spark SQL
dek: Choose the right abstraction for a data engineering pipeline.
idea: For structured ETL, start with DataFrames or SQL: the schema and expressions give Spark information it can optimize.

sections.title: A schema is part of the contract
sections.body: A DataFrame is organized into named, typed columns. Define the expected schema when ingestion needs to be predictable. Check nullability, malformed records, and type conversions explicitly instead of assuming that successful reading means clean data.

sections.title: Where RDDs fit
sections.body: RDDs expose lower-level distributed collections. They are useful for custom processing that does not fit structured expressions. Python DataFrames do not provide the Scala/Java typed Dataset API. In an interview, separate the concepts from language-specific API names.

sections.title: SQL or DataFrame?
sections.body: These are two ways of expressing structured computation through Spark SQL. Choose the form your team can maintain, then inspect the plan. Equivalent logic may produce equivalent plans; switching syntax alone is not a performance strategy.

code:
orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("Pune", 500), ("Delhi", 700), ("Pune", 300)],
    "city string, amount long"
)
orders.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")
spark.sql("""
    SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY city ORDER BY city
""").show()
pitfall: A DataFrame has no guaranteed row order unless you request ordering. Do not rely on the display order of a small test.
question: Is Spark SQL slower than the DataFrame API?
answer: Not inherently. Both use Spark SQL’s engine. Compare the optimized and physical plans for equivalent expressions, plus runtime metrics and UDF use.

sources.title: DataFrames, SQL, and Dataset language support

title: Lazy evaluation & actions
dek: Understand why a line of code is not a job.
idea: Transformations describe a computation. An action asks Spark to produce a result, triggering the work it needs.

sections.title: Build a plan, then execute
sections.body: Think of a transaction pipeline as a recipe: read, filter, select, aggregate. Describing a recipe is different from cooking it. Deferring execution lets Spark inspect the requested computation before running it.

sections.title: Predict before you run
sections.body: In this example, building even describes a filter. count() asks for a result. A second action can require work again unless an appropriate intermediate result has been persisted and materialized.

sections.title: Use the plan as evidence
sections.body: explain("formatted") helps you inspect execution operators without collecting the dataset. Distinguish planning from execution, and avoid claiming that every API call is free: schema inference and metadata operations can do work too.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
numbers = spark.range(0, 10)
even = numbers.filter(F.col("id") % 2 == 0)
even.explain("formatted")
print(even.count())
output: count() returns 5. The plan contains a range and a filter.
pitfall: Do not say “one action always equals exactly one Spark job.” SQL execution, subqueries, and adaptive execution can make that relationship more involved.
question: I wrote five transformations. How many jobs did I create?
answer: Transformation count alone cannot tell you. Ask which actions run, inspect the executed plan, and confirm in the Spark UI. Lazy transformations primarily build a plan.

title: Jobs, stages & tasks
dek: Read the execution hierarchy without memorizing misleading formulas.
idea: An application runs jobs. Jobs are split into stages, and a stage has tasks that process its partitions.

sections.title: Work at three scales
sections.body: A job is work initiated to obtain a result. A stage groups tasks that can run without crossing a shuffle dependency. Within a stage, tasks operate on partitions. Task attempts can be retried, so attempts and distinct tasks are different counts.

sections.title: Partitions are not CPU cores
sections.body: In the simplified case of 12 ready tasks and four available task slots, execution needs at least three waves. That assumes one slot per task, similar task lengths, and no failures. Twelve partitions do not imply twelve machines.

sections.title: Read the UI from the slow end
sections.body: Find the slow stage, compare task durations, and inspect input sizes and shuffle metrics. One unusually slow task suggests a different investigation from every task being slow. Use evidence to distinguish imbalance from insufficient overall resources.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
events = spark.range(0, 120, 1, 4)
counts = (events.withColumn("bucket", F.col("id") % 3)
          .groupBy("bucket").count())
counts.explain("formatted")
counts.orderBy("bucket").show()
output: Buckets 0, 1, and 2 each have count 40. Exact job/stage counts depend on the executed plan and configuration.
pitfall: A partition is a unit of data; a task is a unit of execution. AQE can change the number of downstream shuffle partitions.
question: You have 200 tasks and 20 available slots. Will the stage take exactly ten task durations?
answer: Ten waves is only a lower-bound model for uniform tasks with no overhead. Skew, scheduling, I/O, retries, and contention affect actual completion time.

title: Partitions & shuffles
dek: Follow the data when work needs to cross partition boundaries.
idea: A shuffle redistributes records across partitions. It is often necessary when records sharing a key must meet.

sections.title: Local work versus redistribution
sections.body: A filter can evaluate rows where they already are. A grouped aggregation needs values for each key brought together. Spark can sometimes reduce data locally first, but the remaining partial results still need appropriate distribution.

sections.title: Repartition or coalesce?
sections.body: repartition redistributes data through a shuffle. coalesce can reduce the partition count without a shuffle, but a drastic reduction can constrain parallelism. Neither operation is a universal fix for output file sizing.

sections.title: Partitioning has several meanings
sections.body: An execution partition is not the same as a storage directory such as date=2026-09-13. Input files, execution partitions, shuffle partitions, and output files are related through execution and writer behavior; they are not interchangeable counts.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
rows = spark.range(0, 12, 1, 3)
keyed = rows.withColumn("key", F.col("id") % 2)
redistributed = keyed.repartition(4, "key")
redistributed.explain("formatted")
output: Look for an Exchange with hash partitioning on key. Four requested partitions do not guarantee four nonempty partitions.
pitfall: More partitions can improve parallelism, but too many tiny tasks add overhead. A hot key can remain hot after repartitioning by that same key.
question: Why did coalesce(1) make my write slow?
answer: It funnels output through one partition and can reduce upstream parallelism. Check file requirements; prefer a useful number of output partitions. A shuffle before the final write trades extra redistribution for parallel upstream work.

title: Joins & data skew
dek: Reason about data shape before reaching for a join hint.
idea: Choose a join strategy using data sizes, key distribution, and the actual execution plan—not table names.

sections.title: Start with correctness
sections.body: Identify the join keys, join type, null behavior, and expected row count. Duplicate keys can multiply output rows. A fast join that changes business grain is still wrong.

sections.title: Small side, large side
sections.body: A broadcast join distributes a build-side relation to executors. It can avoid shuffling the large side for a suitable join, but the broadcast must fit safely. Filter and project the small relation before assessing size. Hints are requests with strategy limitations, not guarantees.

sections.title: When one key dominates
sections.body: If most events share one customer key, hashing that key still sends its records together. Diagnose task and partition imbalance. Possible responses include isolating hot keys, pre-aggregation where valid, or carefully designed salting. Check correctness when combining salted results.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
facts = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 100), (2, 200)],
                              "customer_id long, amount long")
customers = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Pune"), (2, "Delhi")],
                                  "customer_id long, city string")
joined = facts.join(F.broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
joined.explain("formatted")
joined.orderBy("customer_id").show()
output: Two matching rows: customer 1 / 100 / Pune and customer 2 / 200 / Delhi.
pitfall: Do not broadcast a relation simply because it is smaller than the other table. Its expanded size and executor memory pressure matter.
question: A join finishes 199 tasks quickly and one task takes 20 minutes. What do you inspect?
answer: Compare the slow task’s input and shuffle size, spill, and execution time. Check hot or null keys and join multiplicity. Consider adaptive skew handling where applicable; do not assume that adding executors splits a single hot partition.

title: Caching & fault tolerance
dek: Reuse the right work, and know what Spark can recompute.
idea: Caching is a reuse decision. Recovery relies on the ability to recompute missing work from available inputs.

sections.title: Cache a reusable boundary
sections.body: If several actions reuse an expensive filtered dataset, persisting that intermediate result may help. Materialization costs time and storage. Compare total runtime, check the Storage tab, and release data when its reuse window ends.

sections.title: Be precise about defaults
sections.body: In PySpark 3.5.7, DataFrame cache() uses MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER. Do not transfer this default to every RDD API or version. Storage settings and eviction determine what remains available for reuse.

sections.title: Recovery has boundaries
sections.body: Spark can recompute lost RDD partitions using lineage. That requires usable upstream inputs; it does not promise that every external side effect runs exactly once. Retry-aware writes, deterministic logic, and appropriate transactional sinks are separate design decisions.

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
reusable = spark.range(100).filter(F.col("id") % 2 == 0).cache()
try:
    print(reusable.count())  # materializes this small example
    reusable.agg(F.sum("id").alias("total")).show()
finally:
    reusable.unpersist()
pitfall: Calling cache() alone does not eagerly materialize the dataset. Cached data can also be evicted or lost.
question: Is caching every DataFrame a good way to speed up my pipeline?
answer: No. Identify repeated expensive computation, memory capacity, and reuse lifetime. Caching one-use intermediates can add overhead and pressure. Measure, inspect storage, and unpersist deliberately.

title: The complete Spark execution flow
dek: From spark-submit to the final result: explain who does what, when, and why.
idea: Tell two connected stories: how the application gets compute, and how a query turns a plan into work on that compute.

sections.title: Before you draw the flow
sections.body:
Open with a scope statement: “I’ll describe a classic PySpark batch application using DataFrames on Spark 3.5.7.” Then separate the application’s lifetime from the execution of an individual query. One application can run many queries and jobs.

This matters in interviews: a notebook may already have a session and compute attached. With Spark Connect, a client sends plans to a remote server; the Python client is not the classic driver described below. Structured Streaming adds a continuously running query and its own execution lifecycle.

Learn the eight fundamentals first if the terms are new. This is the capstone that connects them.

Check the source: Spark Connect has a separate client/server architecture · Application components and resource allocation

sections.title: 1–4 · Start the application
sections.body:
1. Submit the program. A command such as spark-submit app.py launches the application using its master and deployment configuration. In client mode the driver runs on the submitting side; in cluster mode the cluster infrastructure launches it. The deployment mode determines driver placement.
  2. Initialize or reuse the session. Driver-side code obtains a SparkSession. In classic Spark, it uses a SparkContext for the application’s connection and scheduling machinery. getOrCreate() may return an existing session; it is not a command that always launches a fresh driver.
  3. Acquire executor resources. Cluster-manager-specific integration requests resources. YARN, Kubernetes, and Spark standalone are common choices; Mesos is deprecated in this reference release. Executors are processes, not synonyms for worker machines. Memory requests also have overhead beyond the configured executor heap.
  4. Register and become schedulable. Executors connect back to the driver. Resource availability and readiness settings affect when scheduling begins. There is no universal rule that every requested executor must exist before work can start. Dynamic allocation can add or remove executors later.

In local mode, task threads run locally; there is no remote cluster-manager allocation of three separate executors. In an already attached notebook, much of this startup may have happened before your cell ran.

Check the source: Driver placement and spark-submit · SparkSession.getOrCreate: create or reuse · Application components and resource allocation · Scheduling and dynamic resource allocation · Task CPUs, registration readiness, and retry configuration

sections.title: 5–8 · Describe the query and plan it
sections.body:
1. Run the driver-side program. Python control flow executes normally. Reading a table and building expressions such as filter and groupBy describe a distributed computation. Metadata discovery, schema inference, and analysis can already do work or report errors.
  2. Analyze the logical plan. Spark SQL resolves references to columns, relations, functions, and types. “Aggregate over a filter over an input relation” describes the requested result. A logical input relation is not yet a physical FileScan operator.
  3. Optimize the logical plan. Applicable rules simplify expressions and reduce unnecessary work. Column pruning and eligible filter pushdown are useful examples. Pushdown depends on the source and predicate; a remaining filter may still need to run. Join reordering and strategy choices have eligibility, statistics, and configuration requirements.
  4. Choose and prepare physical operators. The physical plan specifies how to compute the result: scans, filters, partial/final aggregates, joins, and exchanges. Eligible operators can be fused into generated code. That fusion is distinct from a scheduler stage.

These are conceptual planning phases, not an eager timeline for every transformation. Query execution holds lazily evaluated planning results; an action or plan inspection can demand them. explain("extended") lets you inspect the representations before requesting result rows.

Catalyst plans structured queries. The DAG scheduler later works with execution dependencies; it does not schedule the Catalyst logical tree directly. Ordinary RDD transformations do not go through the same DataFrame/SQL optimization pipeline.

Check the source: QueryExecution: analysis, optimization, physical planning · Reading EXPLAIN output · Physical strategy selection and join eligibility

sections.title: 9–11 · Request results and schedule work
sections.body:
1. Call an action. show(), count(), collect(), or an actual write operation asks for an outcome. Accessing df.write alone only creates a writer. Necessary planning is completed and execution work is submitted. One user action can lead to multiple scheduler jobs; query execution and job are different levels.
  2. Build the stage dependencies and tasks. The DAG scheduler identifies shuffle dependencies and available intermediate results. For a runnable stage attempt, it creates the required tasks and submits them as a TaskSet. A ShuffleMapStage produces shuffle output; a ResultStage produces the result requested by that job.
  3. Place task attempts on executors. The task scheduler uses resource offers, locality preferences, scheduling policy, and task resource requirements. The scheduler backend dispatches the selected work to executors. The cluster manager supplies resources; it is not an obligatory relay for each task or each data row.

Say “one task per partition to compute in that stage attempt”, not “one task per original file.” Some actions need only a subset of partitions. Retries and speculation create additional attempts, and downstream partition counts can change.

CPU-only illustration: three executors, four available cores each
Task CPU requestAvailable task slots16 ready tasks need at least
spark.task.cpus = 13 × floor(4 / 1) = 122 waves
spark.task.cpus = 23 × floor(4 / 2) = 63 waves

This is a capacity model, not a timing promise. Other resources, competing jobs, skew, and task durations matter. Tasks run on executor threads; Spark does not permanently pin a partition to a physical CPU core.

Check the source: Actions, lazy transformations, and recomputation · DAGScheduler: stages, tasks, TaskSets, and recovery · TaskSchedulerImpl: task placement and resource offers · Task CPUs, registration readiness, and retry configuration

sections.title: 12–14 · Process partitions and shuffle
sections.body:
1. Execute the task’s computation. An executor deserializes task information and processes the assigned execution partition. Pipelined operators can read, filter, project, and partly aggregate within one task. Built-in SQL expressions run through Spark’s execution engine; Python UDFs can involve Python worker processes.
  2. Produce and fetch shuffle blocks when required. For a grouped sum, map-side tasks may first produce partial sums. A shuffle exchange distributes these by key. The same key must reach compatible downstream grouping, but multiple distinct keys can share a hash partition. Downstream tasks fetch the required blocks, locally or remotely.
  3. Run downstream operators; adapt when applicable. Once dependencies are available, downstream tasks complete the aggregation. With AQE enabled, materialized exchange statistics can inform changes such as coalescing shuffle partitions or selecting a different supported join strategy. Initial and final plans can differ.

Shuffle can involve serialization, disk I/O, network I/O, and spill. A network transfer is not required for every block. BroadcastExchange instead prepares and distributes a broadcast relation; treating every operator containing “Exchange” as a shuffle is inaccurate.

Locality tries to avoid avoidable movement. PROCESS_LOCAL, NODE_LOCAL, RACK_LOCAL, and ANY describe locality choices; NO_PREF means there is no locality preference. Object-storage reads do not imply that an executor lives beside an HDFS block.

Check the source: Shuffle dependencies and output partitioning · BroadcastExchange is a different exchange · Adaptive query execution and shuffle partition coalescing · Data locality and its trade-offs

An AQE query stage is a physical-plan unit around an exchange; a whole-stage codegen region is an operator-fusion unit. Neither is interchangeable with a DAG scheduler stage in the Jobs/Stages UI. See the AQE query-stage implementation.

sections.title: 15–17 · Observe, recover, and finish
sections.body:
1. Track progress throughout execution. Task status updates and metrics feed the driver’s view of the application. Use the SQL tab for query plans and linked jobs; use stage/task views for skew, shuffle, spill, duration, and GC evidence. The Storage tab concerns materialized persisted data.
  2. Recover eligible failures. A failed task attempt may be retried within configured limits. Lost shuffle output can require recomputation of earlier work. Recovery needs available inputs and recomputable logic; a deterministic code error will not be repaired by simply retrying it. Driver failure is a different lifecycle problem, not a task retry.
  3. Return or commit the output. show() brings back enough rows to display, although computing those rows can require substantial upstream work. collect() returns all result rows to the driver. Distributed file writes normally write data from executors and coordinate commits; output data need not pass through the driver. One executor does not imply one output file. The application can accept another action, or terminate and release resources.

Do not claim that external side effects happen exactly once merely because Spark retries tasks. Side-effect safety and a sink’s commit guarantees need their own design. Do not stop a shared notebook session just because one query has finished.

Check the source: SQL, Jobs, Stages, Executors, and Storage tabs · DAGScheduler: stages, tasks, TaskSets, and recovery · Actions, lazy transformations, and recomputation

sections.title: Trace the example before running it
sections.body:
The runnable example below creates 12 rows in four input partitions. Each ID determines a country and an amount. Filtering amount > 100 keeps IDs 3–11. Here is the input-side arithmetic:

Initial range partitions and surviving amounts
PartitionInput IDsAfter the filter
P00, 1, 2No surviving rows
P13, 4, 5India 150 · USA 200 · UK 250
P26, 7, 8India 300 · USA 350 · UK 400
P39, 10, 11India 450 · USA 500 · UK 550

In a typical full-input execution, each input partition needs a task, even P0: Spark must evaluate its rows before knowing none survive. Partial sums can be shuffled and merged to produce India 900, USA 1050, UK 1200. The output order is unspecified.

CONCEPTUAL PHYSICAL FLOW · READ TOP TO BOTTOM
Range (4 input partitions)
  → Filter amount > 100
  → Partial aggregate by country
  → Shuffle exchange by country
  → Final aggregate
  → Display a small result

This sketches the aggregation’s shuffle boundary, not an assertion that show() must produce exactly one job and two stages. AQE and result retrieval influence the observed scheduler work. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions does not define the four input partitions in this example.

For your Parquet version, replace the generated input with spark.read.parquet("/orders"). Inspect the actual scan and partitioning instead of assuming one input file means one task. Look for pushed filters and selected columns; do not expect a literal operator-for-operator match with this range example.

Check the source: Reading EXPLAIN output · Shuffle dependencies and output partitioning · Adaptive query execution and shuffle partition coalescing

sections.title: A repeatable way to answer in an interview
sections.body:
1. Scope it. State classic PySpark or Spark Connect, batch or streaming, and whether the application is already running.
  2. Draw the roles. Put the driver beside the cluster manager and executors. Show resource allocation separately from task dispatch and data access.
  3. Walk the query. Use one scan → filter → grouped sum → action example. Identify what is a plan and what actually processes data.
  4. Explain the expensive boundary. Draw the partial aggregate, shuffle write/read, and final aggregate. Say what crosses the boundary.
  5. Size the work with assumptions. Separate input partitions, shuffle partitions, task attempts, and concurrent slots. Then discuss skew and retries.
  6. Verify the story. Name the plan operator or Spark UI evidence you would inspect. Finish with where the result goes and whether the application stays alive.

Practice at two depths: give the answer below in roughly 90 seconds, then walk through the example when the interviewer asks for detail. Avoid reciting 17 steps without explaining who owns each step.

Check the source: SQL, Jobs, Stages, Executors, and Storage tabs

sections.title: Corrections to the supplied explanation
sections.body:
The supplied answer is a useful starting outline. These changes make it safer to use as an interview explanation:

Shortcut in the draftMore accurate explanation
Session/context → driver startsThe driver-side program creates or reuses the classic session/context. Driver placement comes from deployment mode; attached notebooks may already have it.
Nothing runs until an actionResult computation is generally lazy. Python code, metadata work, and analysis can run earlier; plan inspection can demand planning.
Every transformation produces a physical plan immediatelyLogical expressions are composed; analysis, optimization, and physical planning are requested as needed.
Task scheduler creates the tasksDAG scheduling creates the tasks and TaskSet for a stage attempt. Task scheduling places and manages task attempts.
One action → one jobA useful first approximation, not a count guarantee. SQL actions can involve multiple jobs.
Exchange → shuffleDistinguish shuffle exchanges from broadcast exchanges.
join is always wide; withColumn is always narrowInspect required physical distribution. Broadcast joins can avoid shuffling the large side; a window expression introduced with withColumn can require redistribution.
Core → one taskTask slots depend on CPU/resource requests and available resources. The default CPU request is one; it is configurable.
Each distinct key gets its own partitionHash partitioning places the same key compatibly, but different keys may share a partition.
The selected physical plan never changesAQE can revise parts of the plan using runtime statistics.

Keep the relationships, but say them precisely: action requests results; shuffle dependencies separate scheduler stages; tasks compute stage partitions; resource slots bound concurrency; executors run task attempts.

Check the source: SparkSession.getOrCreate: create or reuse · QueryExecution: analysis, optimization, physical planning · DAGScheduler: stages, tasks, TaskSets, and recovery · TaskSchedulerImpl: task placement and resource offers · BroadcastExchange is a different exchange · Physical strategy selection and join eligibility · Task CPUs, registration readiness, and retry configuration · Adaptive query execution and shuffle partition coalescing

Further checks: Window distribution requirements · Incremental result retrieval

code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Uses an existing classic SparkSession named spark.
orders = (
    spark.range(0, 12, 1, 4)
    .withColumn("country",
        F.when(F.col("id") % 3 == 0, "India")
         .when(F.col("id") % 3 == 1, "USA")
         .otherwise("UK"))
    .withColumn("amount", F.col("id") * 50)
)
result = (
    orders.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)
    .groupBy("country")
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
)

result.explain("extended")  # inspect plans, not result rows
result.show(truncate=False) # request the result
output: India: 900 · USA: 1050 · UK: 1200. Row order is unspecified. Actual job/stage counts must be observed in the Spark UI.
pitfall: The physical plan, scheduler-stage graph, and task-attempt timeline are different views. Do not infer exact job counts from source lines, or exact concurrency from partition counts.
question: Can you explain the full Spark flow, from application startup to the final result?
answer: For a classic PySpark batch application, submission and deploy mode determine where the driver runs. Driver-side code creates or reuses a SparkSession and SparkContext, and cluster integration obtains executors that register with the driver. DataFrame operations describe a logical query; Spark SQL analyzes it and, when needed, optimizes and plans physical execution. An action requests results and can trigger multiple jobs. The DAG scheduler separates execution dependencies at shuffle boundaries and creates tasks for runnable stage partitions. The task scheduler places task attempts on available executor resources through its backend. Executors run operators, may partly aggregate, and exchange data when the plan requires it. AQE can adjust downstream execution using runtime statistics. Status and metrics return to the driver, recoverable failures can be retried, and the output is returned to the driver or written to storage. The application can then run more work or shut down.

title: Predict what Spark will do
dek: Three interview exercises. Read the code, predict the work, then check your reasoning against the plan and Spark UI.
idea: Predict the distribution each operator needs. State your assumptions before giving a task count, then verify the actual execution.

sections.title: Set the rules before counting tasks
sections.body:
Start after the complete execution-flow lesson. These are original practice exercises for classic PySpark 3.5.7 batch execution. They are not questions reported from an interview and this page does not run Spark.

Use the setup below: four input partitions, four configured SQL shuffle partitions, AQE disabled, no cached/reused query results, and no failed or speculative attempts. We disable AQE only to make the first predictions easier to inspect; this is not a production tuning recommendation. Other versions and managed runtimes can produce different plans.

Each answer gives a source-reviewed expected shape, not an observed execution. Partition counts describe work to schedule; available CPU/resource slots determine how much can run concurrently. Stage IDs, job totals, and durations are runtime evidence.

01 Filter → count02 GroupBy → write03 Join → aggregate

Baseline references: Range partitions · AQE settings · task scheduling

sections.title: One small dataset, three predictions
sections.body:
Run this setup once in a notebook with an existing spark session. Create a local session if needed. A new SQL session keeps these SQL settings separate, but shares the application’s SparkContext and cache. Do not call practice.stop() to clean up the exercise: it would stop the shared context.

PYTHON / PYSPARK
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from uuid import uuid4

# Classic PySpark: use an existing spark session.
practice = spark.newSession()
practice.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
practice.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4")

orders = (
    practice.range(0, 12, 1, 4)
    .withColumn("bucket", F.col("id") % 3)
    .withColumn("amount", F.col("id") * 50)
)

# This default is for local mode on your own machine only.
# On a cluster, replace it with an accessible shared scratch URI.
output_path = f"file:///tmp/spark-fieldnotes-{uuid4().hex}/totals"
print("Spark version:", practice.version)
print("Spark UI:", practice.sparkContext.uiWebUrl)
print("Scratch destination:", output_path)

The write destination above is for local mode only. On a cluster, choose a fresh scratch URI on storage reachable by all participating executors before running exercise 2. The write uses errorifexists, so it will fail if you reuse an existing destination. Rerun the setup to create a new local destination.

IDs 0–11 form four input partitions: 0–2, 3–5, 6–8, and 9–11. Each row has bucket = id % 3 and amount = id × 50. The filter in every exercise retains IDs 3–11.

Setup references: SQL session isolation · Range API · write modes

# After the shared setup, compare AQE on the grouped query.
# Rebuild the query so it uses the changed SQL configuration.
practice.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
try:
    adaptive_totals = (
        orders.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)
        .groupBy("bucket")
        .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
    )
    adaptive_totals.explain("formatted")  # Initial plan
    adaptive_rows = adaptive_totals.collect()  # Only three rows
    adaptive_totals.explain("formatted")  # Inspect final adaptive plan
    print(adaptive_rows)
finally:
    practice.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
output: The same three bucket totals: 0 → 900, 1 → 1050, 2 → 1200, in unspecified order. Compare initial and final plans and observed downstream task counts. AQE may coalesce shuffle partitions; do not prescribe an exact adaptive task count.
pitfall: Do not compare unrelated runs: the optional read-back, show(), collect(), or another action can create additional work. Inspect the SQL execution associated with the action you are explaining. WholeStageCodegen labels and AQE query stages are not scheduler stage IDs.
